lead: An alternator turns engine rotation into electrical power, but not all input becomes output. Copper, iron, diode, brush and mechanical losses turn some input into heat and noise. Efficiency is useful output power divided by input power. The voltage regulator holds the bus voltage steady by adjusting field current. Every vehicle charging system uses this balance: at cruising speed the regulator holds the bus near 14 V whatever the load, while at idle with headlights on the alternator may reach its limit and the bus sags towards battery voltage. This chapter connects loss accounting to regulator action.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.7 for alternator construction and curves, plus basic power and efficiency.

blocks.text: An alternator takes mechanical power P<sub>in</sub> from the engine belt. It delivers electrical output power P<sub>out</sub> = V × I, where V is the regulated bus voltage in volts and I is the load current in amperes. The input splits into output and losses.

items: Stator copper loss: I²R heating in the stator windings. Field copper loss: I<sub>f</sub>²R<sub>f</sub> heating in the field winding, where I<sub>f</sub> is field current in A and R<sub>f</sub> is field resistance in Ω.
Iron loss: hysteresis and eddy-current loss in the stator core. The changing magnetic flux causes it. Laminated cores reduce eddy loss.

Diode loss: in the three-phase bridge, two diodes conduct at a time. P<sub>di</sub> ≈ 2 × V<sub>F</sub> × I<sub>dc</sub>, where V<sub>F</sub> is forward drop per diode in V and I<sub>dc</sub> is DC output current in A. Silicon power diodes have V<sub>F</sub> about 0.7 V to 1.0 V.
Brush and slip-ring loss: field current crosses the brushes. P<sub>brush</sub> ≈ I<sub>f</sub> × V<sub>brush</sub>, where V<sub>brush</sub> is total brush contact drop in V.
Bearing and fan windage loss: friction in bearings and air movement by the fan. It rises with speed.

blocks.text: P_in = P_out + P_cu + P_fe + P_di + P_mech
blocks.where: P_in is mechanical input power in W; P_out is electrical output power in W; P_cu is total copper loss (stator plus field) in W; P_fe is iron loss in W; P_di is diode loss in W; P_mech is the brush-contact loss P_brush plus bearing and fan loss, in W.
η is efficiency in percent; P_out is useful electrical output power in W; P_in is mechanical input power in W.

blocks.text: Use the bus voltage under load for P<sub>out</sub>. Losses are input minus output. A loss budget shows where heat is produced and why the alternator needs cooling.

The regulator holds the bus voltage near a setpoint, about 14 V for a 12 V system. It senses bus voltage, compares it with a reference, and drives the field winding. More field current gives more magnetic flux and higher generated voltage.

An electromechanical regulator uses a voltage coil and vibrating contacts. An electronic regulator uses a Zener reference, comparator, driver transistor and freewheeling diode. Most modern vehicles use electronic regulation.

blocks.where: D is the field PWM duty cycle, no unit, from 0 to 1; t_on is switch-on time in s; t_off is switch-off time in s.
I_f,avg is average field current in A; D is duty cycle; V_bus is bus voltage in V; R_f is field resistance in Ω.

blocks.text: The regulator switches the field on and off quickly. This is field PWM. If voltage falls when lights switch on, the comparator increases D. Field inductance slows the response. Temperature compensation lowers the setpoint when the battery is hot, which reduces overcharging.
Overvoltage protection acts if the regulator or sensing wire fails. It can clamp the field drive off or protect sensitive loads.

Regulator versions. The oldest are contact (vibrating) regulators, in which a voltage coil opens and closes a contact in the field circuit. Hybrid regulators kept the contact as a sensor but switched the field with a transistor. Electronic regulators were first built from discrete transistors and are now monolithic integrated circuits fixed to the brush holder inside the alternator. Multifunction regulators add a load-response function, which ramps up the field slowly when a big load switches on so the engine idle speed does not dip, and an interface (often LIN) through which the engine ECU can set the voltage.

items: Load the alternator and record bus voltage V in V and load current I in A.
Compute output power P_out = V × I in W.
Estimate each loss: copper from winding resistance and current; iron from test data; diode loss as 2 × V_F × I_dc; brush and mechanical loss from test data.
Add the losses and find input power: P_in = P_out + total loss.

blocks.text: In service, a hot rectifier points to diode loss. A hot stator points to copper or iron loss. Bearing noise points to mechanical loss. The loss budget tells whether to change the winding, the diode bridge or the cooling.

examples.question: A 12 V alternator delivers 14.0 V at 70 A to the vehicle bus. The mechanical input power measured at the pulley is 1.30 kW. Find the electrical output power, the total loss, and the efficiency. State units.
steps: Given V = 14.0 V, I = 70 A, P_in = 1.30 kW = 1300 W.
Output power: P_out = V × I = 14.0 V × 70 A = 980 W.
Total loss: P_loss = P_in − P_out = 1300 W − 980 W = 320 W.
examples.answer: The output power is 980 W, the total loss is 320 W, and the efficiency is 75.4%.
examples.check:
V = 14.0
I = 70.0
P_in = 1300.0
P_out = V * I
losses = P_in - P_out
eta = P_out / P_in * 100
print(f"{P_out:.1f}")
print(f"{losses:.1f}")
print(f"{eta:.1f}")

examples.question: For the same alternator (14.0 V, 70 A, 1300 W input), the field winding has R<sub>f</sub> = 3.0 Ω and carries 4.0 A; each stator phase has 0.007 Ω and, in the star-connected bridge, carries an RMS current of 0.816 × I<sub>dc</sub>; each diode drops 0.9 V. (a) Find the PWM duty cycle that gives 4.0 A of field current. (b) Find the field copper loss, the stator copper loss and the diode loss. (c) Find what is left of the total loss for iron, brush, bearing and fan loss.
steps: Duty cycle: I<sub>f,avg</sub> = D × V<sub>bus</sub> ÷ R<sub>f</sub>, so D = I<sub>f</sub> × R<sub>f</sub> ÷ V<sub>bus</sub> = 4.0 × 3.0 ÷ 14.0 = 0.857 (the field is switched on 85.7 % of the time).
Field copper loss: I<sub>f</sub>² R<sub>f</sub> = 4.0² × 3.0 = 48 W.
Stator phase current: 0.816 × 70 A = 57.1 A RMS. Stator copper loss = 3 × 57.1² × 0.007 = 68.5 W.
Total loss from the first example: 320 W. Remainder for iron, brush, bearing and fan loss = 320 − 242.5 = 77.5 W.
The diodes are the largest single loss (126 W, 39 % of the 320 W), which is why the rectifier has its own heat sink in the air stream.
examples.answer: The regulator runs the field at a duty cycle of 0.857; field copper loss is 48 W, stator copper loss 68.5 W and diode loss 126 W, leaving 77.5 W for iron, brush, bearing and fan loss.

traps: Using battery open-circuit voltage instead of the regulated bus voltage under load for P_out.
Treating losses as output. Losses are P_in − P_out; efficiency uses P_out ÷ P_in, not P_out divided by one loss.
Forgetting that two diodes conduct at the same time in the three-phase bridge. Diode loss is about 2 × V_F × I_dc.
Saying the regulator changes stator turns or pulley ratio. It changes field current, usually by PWM.
Mixing mechanical input power in hp with electrical watts. Convert 1 hp = 746 W before using the power balance.

quiz.q: State four loss mechanisms in an alternator.
quiz.a: Copper loss, iron loss, diode loss, and mechanical loss such as brush, bearing and fan loss.

quiz.q: Why does increasing field current raise the alternator output voltage?
quiz.a: More field current gives more magnetic flux. A stronger flux cuts the stator coils and induces a higher generated voltage, so the regulated output rises until the regulator reduces field current.

quiz.q: An alternator delivers 13.8 V at 55 A. Input power is 1.05 kW. Find output power and efficiency.
At idle, bus voltage is 13.2 V with headlights on; at 2000 rpm it is 14.2 V. Explain the regulator action.
quiz.a: At idle, alternator speed is low, so output is limited and the regulator may sit at maximum duty. As speed rises, the same field current gives more output, so the regulator reduces duty to hold the setpoint. A low idle voltage can be normal; check belt and wiring if it stays too low.

quiz.q: A diode bridge uses two conducting diodes, each with V_F = 0.9 V. Output current is 60 A. Estimate diode loss.
Why does the regulator reduce the setpoint when the battery is hot?
quiz.a: A hot battery needs a lower charging voltage to avoid overcharging and excess gassing. Temperature compensation protects battery life.

quiz.q: An alternator with the same output runs hotter after repair. Name two possible loss causes and one check.
quiz.a: Higher diode loss from a poor diode or bad connection; higher copper loss from a narrow winding or loose terminal. Check diode bridge temperature and terminal voltage drop under load.

beyond: Not for the exam. Production cars use smart charging, where the engine control unit sets the alternator voltage from battery temperature and load, sometimes over a LIN link. Regenerative braking raises the setpoint during deceleration to recover energy. Efficiency maps guide 48 V mild-hybrid designs.
